archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A quarterback who holds the ball looking for something downfield and, when it isn't there, gets his value by escaping and running rather than by designed runs or timing throws.

report.headline: His scrambles covered for the sacks, but the passing never stabilized, and now he's hurt
report.take:
Willis got his first real run as a starter this year, eight games for a 1-7 Dolphins team, and the picture is clearer than the two tiny, glittering Green Bay cameos suggested. Those cameos had a 21.985 CPOE in 2025 and a 0.238 EPA per play in 2024 on a handful of games. This season his completion rate over expected sits at -5.06 (42nd of 54), and against last season his CPOE is down 27 points. That isn't a collapse. It's the small-sample shine wearing off. He is a below-average thrower whose real value sits in what happens when the play breaks down.

That value is real. His raw passing EPA totals -16.5, but all of his dropbacks together come to just -3.2. The gap is the scrambles: 24 of them for 211 yards, 12 first downs and 0.668 EPA each. His designed runs are poor (1.92 yards a carry, a third of them stuffed), so this isn't a scheme-built run game. It's improvisation. The cost is the sacks. He takes 3.06 seconds to throw, turns 34.3% of pressures into sacks, and has a 10.3% sack rate (43rd of 54). Every season in his career shows the same pressure-to-sack problem, so this is who he is, not a line issue. On balance the scrambles pay for the sacks, but only just.

The passing profile is stranger than the bottom line. Throws in the short and intermediate zones are good: 0.179 EPA at 0-9 air yards and 0.279 at 10-19, with a 0.9 CPOE in that middle band. The damage comes at both ends. Throws behind the line cost -9.5 EPA in total; screens and swings simply aren't working for him. The deep ball hits only 22.2% of the time, with a -15.8 CPOE and three interceptions. Add three lost fumbles (50th of 54) and five turnover-worthy fumbles, and the drives he kills come from the edges of his game, not the middle.

The last three games looked like progress: 0.065 EPA per dropback, 0.137 better than his season. But that stretch leans on a +10.5 game against the Jets' 30th-ranked defense, and he followed it with -8.2 against Detroit. Then the core injury hit. He is on IR with a December 13 estimated return, surgery still undecided, and Kyle McCord started Week 10. Whether he even gets the job back is now the main question.

strengths.title: Scrambles rescue broken dropbacks
strengths.body: When the pocket fails he escapes and gains real yardage. His scrambles move the chains often enough to nearly erase the hole his passing digs. That has held across every stop of his career and should survive his return, unless the core injury saps his burst, which is the thing to check when he's back.

strengths.title: Efficient in the short-to-intermediate band
strengths.body: Between 0 and 19 air yards he is a positive passer. The intermediate throws are especially productive and land at an above-expected completion rate. On a team that passes far less than its situations call for, this is the part of his game that can carry a functional offense.

strengths.title: Production through Douglas and Dulcich
strengths.body: His best results come throwing to Caleb Douglas and tight end Greg Dulcich, both well into positive EPA per target. Feeding those two over the low-efficiency slot looks is a sustainable path, since it matches his intermediate strength.

concerns.title: Sacks are a career-long trait
concerns.body: He holds the ball, takes pressure, and goes down at one of the league's worst rates. Every past season shows the same pressure-to-sack number, so this is his style, not a blocking problem that a healthy line fixes. The scrambles mostly offset it, but drives stall when the escape doesn't come.

concerns.title: Deep ball and screens bleed points
concerns.body: The two ends of the field are where he loses. Deep throws rarely connect and produce interceptions, and throws behind the line are badly below expected, likely timing and placement on screens rather than scheme alone. Both drag down an otherwise usable middle game.

concerns.title: Ball security beyond the interceptions
concerns.body: Three lost fumbles rank near the bottom, and five turnover-worthy fumbles say it isn't just bad bounces. Some of that is the price of extending plays, but fumble recovery luck tends to even out while the exposure from holding the ball does not.

trend.note: He swung from a -10 EPA game against Minnesota's top defense to +10.5 against the Jets, then back to -8.2 against Detroit. The better last-three numbers rest heavily on one soft opponent, and the injury halted everything.

nextGame.headline: Willis is on IR; Miami goes to Buffalo without him
nextGame.body:
Willis won't play. He's on injured reserve with a core injury and an estimated return of December 13, and McCord started last week. For context, this is a bad spot for any Miami quarterback: Buffalo is a 16.5-point favorite, and its defense hits quarterbacks at the third-highest rate in the league. That would feed straight into Willis's hold-and-escape habit. Buffalo's offense also ranks third in EPA, which points to a trailing, pass-heavy script.

Miami's center Aaron Brewer, an every-snap starter, is out with a concussion, and receiver Chris Bell is out too, so whoever starts faces interior pressure with a thinner receiver group. Buffalo's corners Christian Benford and Dee Alford are both questionable after leaving their last game, which could open the outside. The early forecast shows gusts near 27 mph, worth watching but too far out to lean on.

keyMatchups.title: Buffalo's pass rush hits often
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo's defense ranks third in QB hit rate. For Willis, with his long time to throw and high pressure-to-sack rate, this is the worst kind of opponent. It matters for McCord now and for Willis in the rematch later.

keyMatchups.title: No starting center for Miami
keyMatchups.body: Brewer has played every snap this season and is out. His backup, Andrew Meyer, is himself coming off a stinger. That weakens the interior protection that any Dolphins quarterback needs against this rush.

nextGame.watch: The IR timeline: any update on whether Willis needs surgery decides if a December return, and a shot at the job, is realistic.

restOfSeason.body:
The first question is availability, not efficiency. The return date is an estimate, surgery hasn't been ruled out, and the depth chart now lists him second. If he returns and reclaims the job, expect the same shape. The scrambling and middle-of-the-field throwing will keep him from disaster, the sacks will stay high because they always have, and the passing ceiling is capped by a run-leaning offense near the bottom in pass rate over expected. Roughly 150-200 passing yards with 15-35 rushing yards a game is the honest range. A core injury is exactly the kind that could dent the scrambling that props up his value.

The pieces most likely to move are the deep-ball and screen numbers, which have room to improve toward normal, and the fumbles, which should cool. The pieces that won't move are the sack rate and the below-expected accuracy. Neither the Packers cameos nor the Jets game describe the true talent. The full eight-game body does.
swingFactors: Whether surgery is needed and the December return holds
Whether McCord keeps the job in the meantime
Whether his scrambling burst survives the core injury

confidence.note: On IR with an uncertain timeline, behind McCord on the depth chart, and only eight starts of evidence.
